title: Chapter 115
content:
That had been the plan, but they didn't get the chance to test it out that night. Duty called first, and Lan Wangji had to go visit Lan Xichen for a long, overdue heart-to-heart with his brother, who had been holed up in secluded meditation.

Lately, Wei Wuxian had picked up an odd habit: he couldn’t fall asleep unless he was draped directly over Lan Wangji. Flat on his chest, face-to-face, it didn’t matter—without that warm, living mattress underneath him, sleep just wouldn't come. Left to his own devices in the Jingshi, boredom drove him to turn the place upside down, which unexpectedly turned up quite a treasure trove.

Lan Wangji had been obsessively meticulous since childhood. Calligraphy drills, landscape paintings, academic essays—everything was neatly categorized, filed away, and chronologically ordered. Starting from the earliest practice sheets, Wei Wuxian flipped through them with a grin, thoroughly entertained. Lan Qiren’s vermilion grading notes, however, still gave him phantom toothaches. Out of thousands of pages, he managed to unearth exactly one single typo. True to form, the young Lan Wangji had attached an extra sheet behind it, neatly copying out that one offending character a hundred times in penance. Wei Wuxian clicked his tongue in awe. "Poor kid. Write it that many times and the character stops even looking real."

He was just about to dig deeper into the yellowed pages when a soft, amber glow flickered in the dark outside the Jingshi.

No footsteps broke the quiet, but with a practiced roll, Wei Wuxian vaulted onto the bed and yanked the quilt straight over his head. When Lan Wangji pushed the door open, he was met with the picture-perfect illusion of someone fast asleep.

Lan Wangji walked as silently as a ghost on a normal day, but seeing that his companion was "out cold," he curbed his aura even further, easing the door shut without a click. After a brief pause in the dark, he glided toward the bed.

Before he could reach it, the quilt flew up, whipping over his head and swallowing him whole.

Wei Wuxian sprang forward, tackling the muffled bundle straight back onto the mattress. "Hands where I can see 'em! This is a robbery!"

Underneath the cotton, Lan Wangji didn't move an inch. He lay as limp as a corpse, letting Wei Wuxian's hands roam and tug at his clothes with reckless abandon. Finding zero resistance, the fun dried up almost instantly. Wei Wuxian pouted. "Hanguang-jun, would it kill you to fight back a little? If you play dead, where's the thrill?"

A muffled voice drifted out from the bedding. "What do you want me to do."

Wei Wuxian took on the tone of a helpful tutor. "When I pin you down, you shove me off. Snap your knees together, struggle like your life depends on it, and scream for bloody murder..."

"Loud noises are forbidden in the Cloud Recesses."

"Fine, scream quietly! And when I rip at your clothes, you're supposed to fight tooth and nail to keep your collar shut."

The quilt fell into a heavy pause.

"That sounds difficult," Lan Wangji finally said.

Wei Wuxian gaped. "Difficult?!"

"Mn."

"Fine, guess we're swapping, then. You can have your way with me instead—"

Before the words could fully leave his mouth, the world flipped. The blanket went flying, and Lan Wangji had him pinned flat to the mattress.

Having suffocated under the covers, the pristine order of Lan Wangji's hair ribbon and forehead band was slightly askew. A few loose strands spilled across his brow, and his usually porcelain cheeks were dusted with a soft flush. In the dim lamplight, he looked for all the world like a flustered, ruined beauty. Unfortunately, this particular beauty possessed an iron grip that locked onto Wei Wuxian like a steel vice, wringing out an immediate plea for mercy. "Hanguang-jun! Noble Hanguang-jun, have a heart!"

Lan Wangji’s expression remained stone-still, though the reflection of the candlelight flickered wildly in his golden eyes. "Very well."

"Very well what? The handstand? The rough stuff? Hey—watch the robes!"

"You asked for both."

With that, Lan Wangji settled his weight between Wei Wuxian’s spread thighs, pressing down. Seconds ticked by without another move. Perplexed, Wei Wuxian piped up, "Well? What's the holdup?"

Lan Wangji propped himself up a fraction. "Why are you not fighting back?"

Wei Wuxian hooked both legs firmly around his hips, trapping him in place with a wicked grin. "What can I do? The second you come over, my legs just fly open on their own. Can't shut them even if I tried, zero energy to fight. See? It’s hard for both of us... Wait, hold your horses, look at this first."

He fished a piece of paper from his lapel, waving it in his face. "Lan Zhan, explain yourself. How did you manage to mess up such a basic character? Weren't you paying attention to your lessons? What on earth was running through your head all day?"

Lan Wangji glanced at the paper, his deadpan silence speaking volumes: A serial corner-cutter who wrote his drills in chicken-scratch had some nerve lecturing anyone on typos.

Blatantly ignoring the judgment, Wei Wuxian pressed on. "Check the date on the bottom. Let’s see... you were around fifteen or sixteen, right? Making silly blunders at that age, could it be..."

He paused, doing the mental math, only to realize the date aligned precisely with the three months he’d spent causing chaos as a guest disciple in the Cloud Recesses.

Delight sparked across Wei Wuxian’s face. "Don't tell me Second Young Master Lan was slacking on his calligraphy because he had me on his mind?"

Back then, serving detention in the Library Pavilion, Wei Wuxian had spent every afternoon rolling around the floor, playing dead, and harassing Lan Wangji within an inch of his sanity. It was hard not to think about him—even if the sentiment was pure exasperation. Under that kind of relentless psychological warfare, the fact that Lan Wangji had powered through, keeping one eye on his chores and the other on his troublemaker while only botching a single character, was borderline miraculous.

Wei Wuxian sighed with dramatic sorrow. "Look at that, it's always my fault. Blame me for everything, why don't you."

Lan Wangji’s jaw set, his voice tight. "It was your fault."

His breath hitched for a split second, and his hand shot out to snatch the historical blemish back. Loving nothing more than pushing him to the brink, Wei Wuxian promptly shoved the paper deep down the front of his own inner robes. "Take it if you dare."

Lan Wangji reached inside without missing a beat. And didn't pull his hand back out.

Wei Wuxian choked on a laugh. "Alright, I yield!"

They messed around well into the night, and only in the early morning hours did the room finally settle into something resembling peace.

Wei Wuxian remained sprawled on top of him, head tucked into the crook of Lan Wangji’s neck. The scent of cold sandalwood was rich and warm, lulling him into a lazy, heavy fog. Half-lidded, he murmured, "How's your brother holding up?"

Lan Wangji stroked a slow, rhythmic palm down his bare back. After a quiet spell, he answered softly, "Not well."

Both of them were damp with cooling sweat, and the gentle friction of those fingertips sent shivers dancing across Wei Wuxian's skin, coaxing a slight, restless squirm out of him.

"During the three years of my seclusion," Lan Wangji murmured into the dark, "it was always Brother who came to sit with me."

Now, the tables had turned.

Wei Wuxian didn't need to ask what those three years of "seclusion" had really entailed.

He pressed a quiet kiss to the pale curve of Lan Wangji's ear, pulled the quilt over their shoulders, and let the quiet take them.

The next morning, Lan Wangji was up at the crack of dawn, punctual as clockwork.

Over the past few months of traveling together, he had waged a tireless campaign to drag Wei Wuxian’s sleep schedule into the realm of the living, to zero success. By the time the junior disciples dropped off fresh wash water, Lan Wangji was already fully dressed and pristine. He peeled Wei Wuxian out of the blankets and scooped him straight into the wooden tub—where the man simply floated in the warm water, sound asleep.

When Lan Wangji nudged his shoulder, Wei Wuxian caught his fingers, peppering kisses across the knuckles and nuzzling his cheek into the palm before drifting off again. Getting prodded one too many times, he grumbled in protest, hooked an arm around Lan Wangji's neck to drag him down, and planted a few sloppy, half-conscious kisses on his jaw. "Good boy, stop fussing... Be good, just a few more minutes, please..."

He let out a long yawn and slumped his chin over the rim of the tub, out cold once more.

Knowing full well that Wei Wuxian would probably just roll over and find a new spot to snooze even if the room caught fire, Lan Wangji still dutifully began the wake-up routine at five in the morning, enduring dozens of drowsy, random pecks without so much as flinching.

He brought breakfast back to the Jingshi, setting the trays on the low desk usually reserved for ink and paper. Then, he fished the sleeping lump out of the tub, towel-dried him, slipped the layers of robes over his limbs, and tied the sash tight. Only then did he pull a scroll from the shelf, settling down to read in silence.

Right on cue, as nine in the morning approached, Wei Wuxian shot straight up like a reanimated corpse. He sleepwalked across the floor, found Lan Wangji by touch, pulled the man in for a groggy squeeze, and instinctively gave his thigh a firm fondle. A splash of cold water to the face finally cleared the cobwebs, and he shuffled over to the desk.

Crunches echoed as he inhaled an apple in three bites. Eyeing the packed trays, his eyebrow twitched. "Isn't the family banquet today? Can I really eat this much beforehand?"

Lan Wangji smoothed down the hair ribbon and forehead band Wei Wuxian had just rumpled, his tone calm. "Line your stomach first."

Wei Wuxian knew the food here all too well: bland, watery broths where bitter greens reigned supreme, an endless wasteland of boiled roots and medicinal herbs that tasted like brewed tree bark. If the cuisine hadn't been that dreadful, he wouldn't have been plotting to roast Lan Wangji's rabbits as a teenager. A Gusu Lan clan banquet was a guarantee that you'd leave both starving and miserable.

More importantly, he knew the weight the Lan Clan placed on tradition. Being invited to a family banquet was essentially their formal recognition of his place as Lan Wangji’s cultivation partner. Lan Wangji must have worn down Lan Qiren’s stubborn pride for ages to secure that seat.

Wei Wuxian smiled, touched. "Don't worry. I'll be on my absolute best behavior. Won't embarrass you for a second."

Banquet or not, the affair in the Cloud Recesses bore zero resemblance to any gathering Wei Wuxian had ever attended.

In Yunmeng, a Jiang Clan banquet meant dragging out a dozen long tables in the open training grounds of Lotus Pier. Men, women, elders, and kids all crammed together wherever they liked, shouting across the courtyard without an ounce of decorum. The kitchen was hauled outdoors, stove fires roaring and the scent of roasting meat drifting for miles. You grabbed whatever you wanted, and if a dish ran out, the cooks whipped up another batch on the spot.

As for the Lanling Jin Clan, though Wei Wuxian had never attended one of their feasts, their shameless flaunting of wealth was legendary: sword dances by famed masters, coral trees dripping with fine vintages, and carpets of red silk rolling out for miles.

By comparison, a Gusu Lan family banquet was neither lively nor lavish.

The household was infamously suffocating with its etiquette. No talking while eating, no talking in bed. Even before the first dish was served, the hall was locked in total, eerie silence. Aside from quiet bows and low greetings exchanged upon entering, there was no chatter, let alone laughter. Identical white robes, identical cloud-patterned ribbons, identical solemn—if not completely stone-faced—expressions, as though everyone had been stamped out of the exact same wooden mold.

Scanning this sea of walking mourners, Wei Wuxian ignored the dubious, frosty glares darting his way and muttered inwardly, A family banquet? A funeral wake has more life than this.

Lan Qiren and Lan Xichen made their entrance, prompting Lan Wangji, who had been sitting quietly at Wei Wuxian's side, to shift slightly.

Lan Qiren seemed to treat looking at Wei Wuxian as an immediate health hazard, opting instead to stare rigidly into the empty air ahead. Lan Xichen wore his usual gentle, spring-breeze smile, yet beneath the warm facade, Wei Wuxian couldn't help noticing the sect leader looked noticeably gaunt, worn down by the months in seclusion.

Once the clan leaders were seated, Lan Xichen offered a few brief, courteous remarks, and the meal began.

First came the soup.

A pre-meal broth was standard Gusu Lan custom. It arrived in a plain, palm-sized bowl of polished black pottery. Lifting the delicate lid, Wei Wuxian was greeted by a familiar swamp of dull green leaves and fibrous roots floating in clear water.

His eyebrow gave a violent twitch. Scooping up a spoonful, he swallowed it down—and despite all his mental preparation, his eyes squeezed shut as his hand flew to his forehead in silent agony.

It took him several agonizing seconds to recover from the assault on his taste buds. Propping an elbow on the low table, he thought, ...If the founder of the Lan Clan was an ascetic monk, he must have been the suffering kind.

Unbidden, his mind drifted back to the massive cauldrons of lotus root and pork rib soup simmering on the training grounds of Lotus Pier. The rich, savory aroma used to drift for miles, drawing local village kids to hang off the compound walls, drooling at the sight. In that moment, he wasn't sure who deserved more pity: himself, choking down this bitter swill, or Lan Wangji, who had been raised on it since infancy.

Yet looking around the hall, every other Lan disciple drained their bowls with effortless grace, looking thoroughly serene. Leaving half a bowl uneaten felt rude. Besides, among the three thousand—no, four thousand—rules carved on the mountain wall, he recalled a few explicit dietary mandates: No picky eating, no food wasted, no more than three bowls of rice. Ridiculous as they were, he didn't feel like giving Lan Qiren an excuse to scold him just yet.

Steeling himself, Wei Wuxian prepared to tip the cursed concoction back in one go, only to look down and find his bowl completely empty.

Wei Wuxian blinked in sheer bewilderment.

He picked up the small pottery vessel, turning it over in disbelief. Didn't I just take one sip? Is there a leak in the bottom?

The tabletop beneath was clean and dry.

Glancing sideways, he caught Lan Wangji lowering his own empty bowl, quietly replacing the lid. With eyes lowered, the Second Jade of Lan was dabbing a pristine white handkerchief against the corner of his mouth with immaculate calm.

Wei Wuxian remembered distinctly: Lan Wangji had finished his own soup ages ago.

He also noticed that Lan Wangji's dining table seemed a good several inches closer than it had been before the meal started, subtly nudged over when no one was looking.

Wei Wuxian arched a brow, silently mouthing across the gap: Fast hands, Hanguang-jun.

Lan Wangji set the handkerchief down, offered him a brief, unflinching glance, and turned his gaze straight ahead without a trace of guilt.
